habitat.description:
The Amazon river dolphin, or boto, navigates the murky, tanin-stained waters of the Amazon and Orinoco river basins, threading between submerged tree trunks in flooded forests and hunting fish in channels where visibility drops to zero. These remarkable cetaceans have evolved to thrive in one of the most complex freshwater environments on Earth.

During the wet season, river dolphins follow the rising waters into the varzea floodplain forests, swimming between trees in water several metres deep. Their flexible necks and small eyes are adaptations to this cluttered environment, where echolocation replaces sight as the primary sense for navigation and hunting.

In the dry season, dolphins concentrate in the main river channels and deeper lakes, where receding waters trap fish in ever-shrinking pools. The pink coloration of adult males intensifies with age and activity, flushing brighter during social encounters in these seasonal congregations.

threats.name: Dam Construction
threats.description: Hydroelectric dams fragment river systems, isolating dolphin populations and altering water flow, sediment, and fish migration patterns.

threats.name: Mercury Pollution
threats.description: Gold mining releases mercury into Amazonian waterways, bioaccumulating through the food chain to toxic levels in dolphin tissues.

threats.name: Bycatch and Intentional Killing
threats.description: Dolphins are caught in fishing nets and sometimes deliberately killed for use as fish bait or out of perceived competition with fisheries.

threats.name: Deforestation
threats.description: Loss of floodplain forests reduces the seasonal habitat that dolphins use for feeding during high water periods.

threats.name: Water Pollution
threats.description: Agricultural runoff, sewage, and industrial waste degrade water quality throughout the Amazon basin.

cultural_significance.cinema: Pink river dolphins appear in Amazon documentaries as mystical inhabitants of flooded forests, their unusual appearance captivating audiences.
cultural_significance.literature: The boto features in magical realist literature of South America, blurring boundaries between the natural and supernatural.
cultural_significance.mythology: In Amazonian folklore, the boto can transform into a handsome man who seduces women at riverside festivals, explaining unexpected pregnancies.
cultural_significance.media_presence: River dolphins represent the hidden biodiversity of freshwater systems, often featured in documentaries about Amazon threats.
cultural_significance.cultural_paradox: Protected by folklore and superstition for centuries, river dolphins now face threats from the same modernization that erodes traditional beliefs.

hero_stat: 65% population decline in Amazon river dolphins over 20 years

evidence_summary: Amazon documentaries featuring river dolphins have raised awareness of freshwater biodiversity threats, though measuring direct conservation impact is complicated by the remoteness of river dolphin habitat and limited baseline data.

interesting_facts.text: Amazon river dolphins can turn their heads 180 degrees due to unfused neck vertebrae, unique among cetaceans.
Adult males turn increasingly pink with age; the coloring intensifies during social interactions and excitement.
They use echolocation to navigate murky river waters where visibility can be near zero.
River dolphins diverged from oceanic dolphins approximately 24 million years ago.

amazonian_boto_encantado.description: In Amazonian folklore, the boto encantado (enchanted dolphin) transforms into a handsome young man dressed in white who seduces women at riverside festivals. This shapeshifting mythology historically provided protection for river dolphins, as killing one was believed to bring terrible misfortune.
amazonian_boto_encantado.source: Slater, C. (1994). Dance of the Dolphin. University of Chicago Press.

tupi_guardian.description: The Tupi-Guarani peoples regard the boto as a guardian of rivers and fish, a spiritual intermediary between the underwater and human worlds. Fishers believe dolphins guide fish toward their nets when treated with respect, and harming a dolphin brings poor catches.

colonial_encounter.description: European naturalists encountering Amazon river dolphins in the 18th and 19th centuries were astonished by their pink coloration and flexible necks, features unknown in marine dolphins. These observations contributed to understanding cetacean diversity and the independent evolution of freshwater dolphin lineages.
colonial_encounter.source: Best, R.C. & da Silva, V.M.F. (1989). Amazon River Dolphin. In: Ridgway & Harrison (eds) Handbook of Marine Mammals.
